analysis.one_liner: Bars paying women and minorities less for jobs of equivalent skill and effort.
analysis.headline: The Fair Pay Act of 2017 died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a single vote after being referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on April 14, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for an employer to pay lower wages to jobs dominated by women or by people of a particular race or national origin when those jobs require equivalent skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions — even if the jobs are different kinds of work. It would let workers win compensatory and punitive damages, protect employees who ask about or discuss co-workers' wages, require employers with 25 or more workers (15 or more after two years) to report pay rates by sex, race, and national origin to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and apply the same rules to congressional and executive-branch employees. It died without any action after being sent to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Working women and workers of color, whose full-time earnings today average well below white men's for jobs requiring comparable skill and effort — the bill would let them sue for back pay plus compensatory and punitive damages, recover expert-fee costs, and bring class actions, and would shield anyone penalized for discussing or inquiring about wages.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the existing Equal Pay Act, which covers only equal work on the basis of sex, to cover 'equivalent jobs' — different jobs whose combined skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions are equivalent — and adds race and national origin as protected categories [S2][S3].
Adds compensatory and punitive damages on top of back pay, allows expert fees as part of court costs, and lets cases proceed as class actions, giving workers a real financial remedy [S2][S3].
Makes it illegal to fire or punish an employee for inquiring about, disclosing, comparing, or discussing their own wages or another employee's wages [S2][S3].

Requires employers with 25 or more employees (dropping to 15 or more after the first two years) to report pay rates by sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC, with employee confidentiality protected, so wage patterns become publicly visible [S3].
Applies the same wage-discrimination rules to congressional and executive-branch employees under the Congressional Accountability Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face new liability for pay differences across job categories of equivalent skill, additional court-ordered damages and fees in lawsuits, recordkeeping obligations documenting how they set wages, and new pay-reporting filings by race and sex.

drawbacks.text: Comparing the value of dissimilar jobs — a nurse against a machinist, say — requires judgment calls about skill and responsibility that courts and employers could dispute, and the bill invites litigation over those comparisons, with the employer bearing the burden of proving any pay difference is job-related [S3].

Employers would bear compliance costs: preserving records documenting their wage-setting methods, preparing EEOC pay reports broken down by sex, race, and national origin, and re-pricing jobs without reducing anyone's wages to fix a gap [S3].

The bona fide-factor defense (education, training, experience) applies only if the employer shows the factor is job-related and that no reasonable alternative practice would serve the same purpose — a burden shift that makes it harder for employers to justify pay differences, which critics view as tilting the scales too far against businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give workers a meaningful remedy for a documented gap — women working full time earned about 80 cents per dollar earned by men in 2015, with much larger gaps for Black, Native, and Latina women — and would make pay structures publicly visible, while the costs fall on employers in compliance and litigation exposure. The genuine design question is whether courts can fairly compare dissimilar jobs; the bill tries to manage that by letting employers defend pay differences tied to job-related factors, but it would still generate contested lawsuits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on April 14, 2017, and no hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill on April 14, 2017, joined by 33 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S4].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on April 14, 2017 — the only committee assignment it ever received [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no report, and no floor action; the bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, who avoided a new 'equivalent jobs' pay standard, damages exposure, and mandatory wage reporting; no worker received any of the bill's protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided new pay rules

for.name: Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2017 and spoke for it on the House floor upon introduction.

for.name: 33 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 33 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 14, 2017 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the 115th Congress.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the two years it sat on the committee's docket.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 supporters (the sponsor plus 33 cosponsors) were Democrats and no Republican signed on, in a Republican-controlled House; the bill never advanced past a party-line committee referral.

industries.industry: U.S. employers subject to wage-and-hour law (all industries)
industries.note: The bill would create a new legal duty to pay equivalent-skill jobs comparably, with back pay, compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and fee awards for workers who sue, plus retaliation protection for wage discussions. The industry's cost is workers' wage gain.

These employers would face an additional obligation to file annual EEOC reports disclosing wage rates by job classification together with employee sex, race, and national origin, making pay gaps publicly traceable. The reporting burden falls mainly on businesses with 25 or more workers.
